title: Why Story Points Are a Complete Waste of Time
summary: Podcast host weighs story point pros (relative sizing, collaboration, velocity) against cons (opaque to stakeholders, incomparable across teams, gameable) and concludes all estimation is wasted effort.

assertions.quote: Human beings are terrible at accurately estimating the time required to carry out work, even for tasks that they carry out on a regular basis.
This is more accurate for complex or uncertain work and avoids the pitfalls of timebased estimates which can quickly become inaccurate.

verdicts.note: Comparison-based estimation has some support, but experiments do not show story points beating well-calibrated hour estimates.

Few studies exist; relative estimation improved accuracy in some contexts and worsened it in others, and the authors conclude relative predictions are generally not more accurate than absolute ones and bias estimates when tasks differ much in size.

assertions.quote: This promotes a shared understanding of the work and helps uncover hidden complexities and fosters team alignment.

verdicts.note: Molokken-Ostvold found group estimates less optimistic than individual ones; the shared-understanding benefit is widely reported.

Groups of software professionals produced higher and more realistic estimates than their prior individual ones, qualitatively because they identified more activities, and planning poker gave a shared understanding of the work and risks; student groups, by contrast, became more optimistic.

Group discussion of software estimates beat simple averaging because it produced new knowledge about role interactions, but the review rates the evidence for group combination as not strong since discussion can also push estimates toward risk or conservatism.

assertions.quote: This velocity can then be used to make more reliable forecasts about future work

verdicts.note: Velocity forecasts work when scope and team are stable; point inflation and scope churn routinely break them.

Extrapolating from measured early productivity is called 'a simple time prediction model based on highly local data' that few models beat, but reliability is not quantified and relative (point-based) estimation is elsewhere found no more accurate than absolute estimation.

assertions.quote: This makes it impossible to compare the productivity of different teams using story points.
business stakeholders will attempt to hold the team to timelines regardless of story point estimates
I believe all estimates are a waste of valuable time that could be better spent actually building something.

verdicts.note: Estimation has coordination and prioritization value; NoEstimates works in some contexts but not where commitments are needed.

The review's authors reject the NoEstimates position that predictions are a waste as unrealistic, noting that extrapolating progress is itself a time prediction and that judgement-based predictions are on average fairly accurate (20-30% error).

assertions.quote: story points help to shield the team from the emotional pressure and rigidness of fixed timebased commitments

verdicts.note: Padding under pressure is documented, but stakeholders convert points to dates anyway, as the same source notes.

Fibonacci and T-shirt scales speed estimation but gave no accuracy benefit in published and several unpublished experiments and introduce a bias toward the scale's middle value; shielding from deadline pressure is not tested.
